Permanent benches of High Court in Orissa  
*383. SHRI BHAGIRATHI MAJHI: Will the Minister of L AW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government has given any direction to the Orissa Government on establish-
ment of permanent benches of High Court as per the recommendation of Jaswant Singh 
Commission constituted by the Central Government; 
(b)  if so, at which places these benches are being considered and by when; and 
(c)  whether, as per the merger agreement of Mayurbhanj with Orissa and Central Govern-
ment, one of such bench is being planned at Baripad a, the head quarter of Mayurbhanj 
district? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) No, Sir. The 
Government had in 1987, brought to the notice of the State Governments, the recommenda-
tions of the Jaswant Singh Commission fixing norms for setting up of Benches of High 
Courts away from their principal seats.  
(b)  Does not arise.Z 
(c)  No proposal has been received from the State Government for setting up a Bench of 
High Court at Baripada.

SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ: Sir, I would like to inform the hon. Member that in order to set up a 
bench of a High Court away from the principal seat, there has to be a recommendation from the 
Governor, the Chief Justice and thereafter the President issues notification to that effect. As a I have 
submitted, there is no proposal pending with us from the State Government after having consulted 
the constitutional authorities of the State. So, there is no question of the Central Government or the 
President issuing a notification. Once such recommendations are received from the Orissa 
Government, and after consultations with the Chief Justice of the High Court, we will take 
action.

SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ: Sir, this is not by way of agreement; it is the constitutional position 
that if there is a High Court and a sitting of the High Court has to take place at any place other than 
the High Court, the recommendation must come from the Chief Justice and Governor. After that 
the President issues the notification.  
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: Hon. Chairman Sir, as far as distance goes, most 
of the States of the North-east region are located at a distance of about 2500 kilometres from the 
national Capital, Delhi. Sir, these various States of North Eastern Region, namely, Assam, 
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Manipur, Nagaland are far away from Delhi. The communication 
network between Delhi and this North Eastern Region is yet to be developed. Frankly speaking, Sir, 
a lot is yet to be done. During floods, the entire region of Assam gets totally cut off from the 
mainstream of the country.  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Would you please put the question?  
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: I am coming to the question. Sir, considering the 
distance, time factor as well as mode of communication, it becomes very difficult for any person to 
come to Delhi, to the Supreme Court to settle his legal problems. It is also important to note that 
these States of North Eastern Region have different problems, which need special attention from the 
Centre. Guwahati being headquarters and hub of North Eastern Region ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question.  
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA: Sir, I would like to know whether the 
Government, taking into account the above factors, is seriously considering setting up the Bench 
of hon. Supreme Court at Guwahati.  
SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ: Sir, the question does not relate to the setting up of a Bench of 
Supreme Court. But since North East is a sensitive area, I would like to give some information to the 
hon. Member with regard to solving the problem of the North Eastern Region. Sir, the North Eastern 
Region, these seven-sisters, were asked by me quite some time ago in 1987 or 1988 that they 
could, if they liked, have separate High Court of their own. As there was not much litigation in 
these tribal States, they agreed to take circuit courts. I have already established, in each small 
jurisdictional area, a separate circuit court of Guwahati High Court. As far as the question of 
Bench of the Supreme Court is concerned, that is a separate question, and, for that, the reply would 
be totally different than what is the scope of this question.  

Oral Answers  [21 APRIL 2008]  to Questions   3 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Hon. Chairman, Sir, if no t in Baripada, that is, 
Mayurbhanj District, whether the Orissa Government has given any proposal for setting up 
a Bench of the High Court at Sambalpur, Berhampur, Rourkela, Baleshwar, Bolangir or any 
other place in Orissa.  
SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ: Sir, in 1991, there was proposa l for setting up a Bench at 
Berhampur and Sambalpur, or, in the alternative, at Bolangir in Orissa. But, after 1999, as 
per the provision of the Constitution, a broad recommendation of the Chief Justice and the 
State Government—which have not yet been received b y us—is required, and, therefore, 
there is no question of Central Government following it up. There has to be a proposal from 
the State Government and the High Court concerned.

Rating of management institutions  
*386. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMURtt 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:  
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government proposes to introduce rating for management institutions, similar 
to international standards such as ISO:9001. to enc ourage their swift movement towards 
achieving excellence; and 
(b)  if so, whether an independent Regulatory Authority for Higher Education would be 
constituted and entrusted with taking a holistic view, so that standards of our higher education, 
technical and management, could be further improved , to enable our students to compete 
successfully in the growing global market? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) No Sir. At present there is no 
such proposal under consideration.  
(b) No Sir.  
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: Sir, management study in India is one of the 
favourite subjects. Even students from abroad are o pting for management course in India. 
But the management study in India is a distant dream for the poor students. So I would like 
to know from the hon. Minister what steps the Government have taken to provide management 
education to poor students.  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, this does not arise out of the main question. It 
does not pertain to the main question.  
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: It is very expensive. The Government should 
take some steps, so that the management education a lso can be given to the poor students. 
With economic growth, demand for trained managerial manpower in all organisations—in 
social, economic and public service activities—is i ncreased sharply. It is essential that our 
business schools and management institutions delive r quality education to meet the new 
challenges and the growing competition. I would like to know from the hon. Minister up to 
what extent today's management education really matches with the business practices.  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, as per section 3G of the AICTE Act, engineering,  
technology, architecture, town planning management, pharmacy, applied arts and crafts are  
all under the purview of the AICTE. The AICTE is empowered under the law to lay down  
• the norms and standards for the institutions whic h impart education in these fields to the

SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: Sir, right now, the hon. Mini ster has dealt with the fee 
structure. But, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister, through you, Sir, to the 
quality of education in the Government institutions . For instance, you can take any State. 
People are encouraging their children to go to private institutions because the general feeling 
is that the standards in Government institutions ar e going down day by day. What are the 
specific steps the Government is intending to take to improve the quality and standards of 
Government educational institutions, especially at the college level?  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, improving standards of education is a continual 
process. Sir, the AICTE has ten Boards of Studies under it, where the Board of Management 
is also one of the Boards. The AICTE is in constant consultation with the industry to ensure 
that the requirements and needs of the industry are  incorporated in the curriculum. Besides 
this, the UGC has also come up with several initiatives to ensure that the quality is assured to 
the students who seek admission into the management institutions.  
SHRI N.K.. SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the National Knowledge Commission has made 
a very coherent set of recommendations which, inter alia, includes the setting up of an 
independent regulatory authority. The hon. Minister  has rather summarily rejected this by 
saying, "No, Sir, there is no such intention". But, we all know that there is a need to have an 
arm's length relationship to do away with the Ministry's micro management of the educational 
system and, therefore, would the Minister like to e xplain as to what are the considerations 
which led to the rejection of this very important recommendation of the National Knowledge 
Commission for setting up of an independent regulatory authority?  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, this would require c onsultation with various 
Ministries and consultations have been on and no co nsensus has yet been reached. This 
would involve various other departments like the MCI, TCI, AICTE, UGC and several others. 
So, unless there is a consensus, we cannot come out  with a conclusion that we would need 
and require an overall arching body such as this. H owever, Sir, until then, let me again 
inform the House, through you, that there is a Comm ittee that has been set up under Prof. 
Yashpalji to look into the working of the AICTE and UGC, and I think, we will have to wait 
for the recommendations.

Declining trend of academic research  
 †*387 .  SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:  
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHL††  
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that the country is still lagg ing behind in the field of academic 
research; 
(b)  whether it is also a fact that research work in the country is negligible, in comparison to 
America, England, France, China, Japan and Germany; and 
(c)  if so, the total number of research papers published by all the above countries at the 
international level in 2005,2006 and 2007? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (c) While there is no study by the Central Government to establish India's position in the 
field of academic research, the Task Force on Stren gthening Basic Science Research in 
Universities under the Chairmanship of Professor M.  M. Sharma set up by the Central 
Government, has observed that there is no formal linkage between universities and national-level 
research institutions and the same should be promoted through joint research projects and training 
and that the number of Ph. Ds in Sciences and Engineering disciplines from Indian Universities 
is quite low vis-a-vis the number of M. Sc/B. Tech when compared to what it is in USA, UK, 
Germany, Japan, etc. The position in regard to academic research in other subjects (non-sciences) 
is also not available. No information is being maintained by the Central Government in regard to 
the number of research papers by other countries including the USA, UK, France, China, 
Japan and Germany.  
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, it is very disappoint ing statement given by  the 
Government. It is now well-known that a survey conducted in 2005 has revealed that the US 
contributes 32 per cent of the research papers published globally, India only contributes 2.5 
per cent to its credit. The number of Ph.Ds awarded in one year in U S is, 25,000,

Representation of non-teaching staff in universities  
*388. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of HUMAN R ESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government is aware of the demand of the All India University Employees 
Confederation, to provide representation to non-teaching employees in the decision-making 
bodies of the universities; 
(b)  if so, whether any steps have been taken by Government; 
(c)  if so, the details thereof; and 
(d)  if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Government is aware of the demand of the All India University 
Employees Confederation to provide representation t o non-teaching employees in the 
decision-making bodies of the universities. A university is established either by the Parliament 
or by the State legislature concerned. Besides, und er section 3 of the University Grants 
Commission Act 1956, the Central Government also declares, upon the advice of the UGC, 
an institution to be 'deemed-to-be-university'.  
While universities established by statutes (both Central and State) function in accordance 
with the provisions of the relevant Acts, the institutions that are granted the status of'deemed-
to-be-university', function as per their Memorandum of Association and Rules of Association. 
These universities take their own decision with reg ard to the composition of their various 
decision-making bodies and as such the Government h as no role with regard to providing 
representation to the non-teaching employees in their decision-making bodies.  
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Sir, it is an era of democratisation. When the workers are 
getting their due place in decision-making in factories, why can't the non-teaching employees 
be given representation in decision-making bodies of universities? Since the UGC is funding 
various universities, can't they give some concrete directive in the form of recommendations 
in order to provide representation to non-teaching employees in the decision-making bodies 
of universities?  

14    Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, the role of UGC is limited to evaluating the kind 
of financial support that the universities require, and based on the requests from universities, 
to disburse the funds to the universities. The univ ersities are autonomous bodies and they 
have a functional autonomy within the broad education policy of the Government. They are 
guided by certain regulations. They can decide whether they would want the non-teaching 
employees on their bodies or not. Respecting the autonomy of universities and institutes, we 
do not have a major role to play in asking them to ensure that there is representation given to 
the non-teaching employees.  
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Sir, the hon. Minister says that there is no role of the 
Government in providing an opportunity to the non-teaching staff of the university. But they 
can always given various recommendations, because they are funding the universities. This 
is one of the demands which is pending for the last  one or two decades. The Government 
should give some sort of a directive to various universities. This is my suggestion.  
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, our role would be li mited to definitely giving 
them the suggestions or the directions and asking them to consider it. Sir, the concerns of the 
hon. Member would definitely  be conveyed to the universities.

Oral Answers  [21 APRIL 2008]  to Questions   17  
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister in regard to 
release of grants for OBC students' scholarship. I would like to know whether there is any 
criterion decided by the Central Government, becaus e I found that there are seven States 
which do not get even a single rupee under this category in 2006-07 as stated in the list given 
by the hon. Minister. I would like to know whether the Government has decided to any 
criterion for this.  
SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR: As has already been explained in the written reply to the 
question, the criterion is that for the grant which  is released to the State, the State should 
send the utilization certificate. If we do not rece ive the utilization certificate, it becomes 
difficult to give the grant the next year. Then, there has to be a provision in the Budget of the 
_State for committed liability. If we find that the Budget of the State does not make a provision 
for committed liability, then also it becomes difficult for the Centre to give grants.  
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: What is the scheme for students belonging to another category, 
the category of students who are economically backward, economically weak and who are 
below poverty-line? I would like to know whether there is any scheme for such students, the 
category mentioned in the question.  
SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR: Sir, the question is not very clear. Do you mean the OBC 
students who are below poverty-line or the general students who are below poverty-line?  
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: My question is about the genera l students who are below 
poverty-line. I would like to know whether you are having any scheme to give this type of 
scholarships to them also.  
SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR: There are poverty alleviation programmes. But my Ministry 
is dealing with the SC and the OBC students. We have set up a Commission to study and 
give a report about the educational and other facilities that can be given to the economically 
backward. But the report is  awaited. At the moment, whatever schemes we have are for the 
OBCs and the SC students.

Committee to examine grid collapse  
*391.    SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA:†† 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether, in view of the recent grid collapse, the C entral Government has set up a 
Committee to come up with preventive measures to sa ve cities from being plunged into 
darkness due to tripping of power carrying lines, by both man-made and natural causes; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof and by when the Committe e is likely to submit its report to 
Government; 
(c)  whether the reasons for grid collapse have been identified and if so, the details thereof; 
and 
(d)  the steps taken by Government to avoid recurrence of such incidents in future? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (d) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (d) A Committee has been set up by the Central Electricity Authority on 13th March, 
2008 to inquire into the partial grid disturbances which occurred in the Northern Region on 
7th and 9th March, 2008. The main reason for trippi ngs of transmission lines prima facie 
was the unusual weather pattern and pollution in th e Region. Unprecedented fog and high 
humidity, coupled with high levels of pollution, further aggravated by the absence of winter 
rains resulted in the unprecedented trippings of transmission lines. The prevailing humidity 
level of above 90%, at that time being far above th e critical level of 75%, was one of the 
major causes of the trippings. As an immediate measure, physical cleaning of insulators in 
the worst affected and most vulnerable areas was initiated to avoid recurrence of the incident 
during the ensuing period. The report is to be submitted by the Committee within two months. 
Remedial measures to avoid reoccurrence of such incidents, as suggested by the Committee, 
would be duly considered by the Government for implementation.  
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Sir, the Minister in his  reply has said that grid 
disturbances have happened largely due to weather c onditions. Sir, such vagaries are not 
unusual in our part of the world and in the rest of the world. Sir, what I would like to ask the 
hon. Minister is realising that these kinds of weather fluctuations happen, have we looked at 
the infrastructure? Sir, whereas we have been using  ceramic or porcelain insulators which 
are not that resistant, has any detailed analysis been undertaken to see the nature of pollutants 
and then, have they thought of upgrading to polymer insulators which will withhold weather 
fluctuations a little better?  
SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE: It has already been decided to go for polymer insulators 
and we are switching from the conventional insulators to polymer insulators now at vulnerable 
places in NCR.  
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: By when would that be done?  
SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE: Cleaning has already been started on the day these 
disturbances have taken place. Also on the day, the incident had taken place on 9th, meeting 
was held and immediately a view was taken, the replacement was already done in some

Cost for generation of solar energy  
*381. SHRI RAJNITI PRASAD: Will the Minister of NEW AND RENEWABLE ENERGY 
be pleased to state:  
(a)  the cost per MW for generation of solar energy; and 
(b)  the steps Government is taking to make solar energy more cost effective? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH):(a) Solar energy can be harnessed through two routes namely; (i) solar photovoltaic 
for direct electricity generation and (ii) solar thermal for heating, cooling and power generation.  
Solar photovoltaic cells convert light in to electricity. A number of solar photovoltaic cells are 
joined to make a solar photovoltaic (SPV) module. SPV modules and interface electronics are used 
in a solar photovoltaic power generating system to harness solar energy for electricity generation. 
Concentrating solar thermal collectors are used to convert solar energy in to steam, which in turn is 
used in conventional turbines for power generation . 

Written Answers to  [ 21 APRIL 2008]  Starred Questions   21  
The estimated capital cost of setting up a solar power plant is in the range of Rs. 16 crore to Rs. 20 
crore per MW and the cost of generation is around Rs. 12 to Rs. 15 per unit, depending upon 
  echnology, efficiency solar insolation etc. 
(b) In order to make solar energy systems more cost effective, the Government has taken several 
steps which include (i) research and development to reduce the costs, improve the efficiency and 
performance of solar energy systems, (ii) incentives to manufacturers, commercial users and 
powers project developers; and (iii) subsidy or soft loans to encourage utilization of solar energy 
systems.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) According to the 
information available with the Central Electricity Authority, the total number of power 
generating stations of the Utilities in the country as on 31st March, 2008 was 445, which 
includes 4 power generating stations located in Delhi.  
Power sub-stations are.in the transmission and distribution segments, depending on the level of 
required voltage transformation and do not add to the capacity of power generation.  
The enhancement in capacity of power generation projects is a continuous process and is 
achieved through addition of new generating capacity as well as Renovation, Modernisation, 
Uprating and Life Extension of operating plants whose performance declines with age. New 
capacity addition during 2005-06,2006-07 and 2007-08 was 3,488.28 MW, 7,074.80 MW and 
9263 MW respectively. The year-wise and power station-wise details are given in the Statement-I.

capacity has been available by virtue of Uprating under the Renovation, Modernization and 
Uprating Scheme during the last three years are enclosed as Statement-II. (See below) Normally this 
exercise is restricted to restoring declining efficiency level of performance.

Generation of renewable energy  
*384. SHRI MAHMOOD A. MADANI: Will the Minister of NEW AND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY be pleased to state:  
(a)  what is the total generation of solar energy and other renewable energy in the country; 
(b)  the estimated plan for production of renewable energy; and 
(c)  what steps Government is taking to increase the capacity to the plan level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) A grid-interactive power generation installed capacity of 11,449 MW based 
on various renewable energy sources has been set up in the country as on 31.01.2008. This 
comprises of 7,939 MW wind power, 2,062 MW small hydro power, 1,446 MW bio-power 
and 2 MW solar power. This apart, a large number of  off-grid/decentralized renewable 
energy systems/devices are making a significant contribution to conservation of conventional 
energy.  
(b) A capacity addition of 15,000 MW from renewable energy sources (14,000 MW grid-
interactive and 1,000 MW off-grid/distributed) has been proposed during the Eleventh Plan 
period.

(c) The Government is promoting development of the renewable energy sector through a 
mix of fiscal and financial incentives that include  capital/interest subsidy, accelarated 
depreciation, nil/concessional excise and customs duties. Further benefit under Section 80-
1A of Income Tax Act 1961 is available to undertakings setup for the generation or generation 
and distribution of Renewable power in India. This apart, preferential tariff for grid interactive

(c) if so, by when a final decision in this regard is likely to be taken?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCE SSING 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) to (c) Min istry of Food Processing 
Industries (MFPI) for development and growth of food processing sector, has developed a 
scheme for providing financial assistance for estab lishment of Mega Food Parks, which 
envisages a well-defined agri/horticultural-processing zone containing state of the art  
 processing facilities with support infrastructure and well established supply chain. The scheme 
aims to provide a mechanism to bring together farme rs, processors and retailers and link 
agricultural production to the market so as to ensu re maximization of value addition, 
minimization of wastages and improving farmers' income. The primary objective of the  
- scheme is to facilitate establishment of an integrated value chain, with processing at the core 
and supported by requisite backward and forward linkages. The scheme is project oriented. 
The locations of the Mega Food Parks have to be selected on demand-driven cluster based 
approach with delineated supply chain and well supported by pre-feasibility studies.  
The Scheme envisages financial assistance in the fo rm of grant-in-aid upto 50% of the 
project cost in general areas and up to 75% of the project cost in special category states 
subject to a maximum of Rs. 50.00 crores or the cos t of approved facilities, whichever is 
lower, for all implementing agencies including priv ate sector. The scheme provides for 
establishment of 30 Mega Food Parks with MFPI finan cial assistance of Rs. 1500 crore 
during the Eleventh Five Year Plan.  
The ownership and management of the Mega Food Park would vest with a Special Purpose 
Vehicle (SPV) in which organized retailers, processors, service providers, farmers etc. may 
be the equity holders or there may be an anchor investor along with its ancillaries, associated 
companies and other stakeholders. The government ag encies may also be shareholders in 
SPV upto a maximum of 49%-. 
The Mega Food Park scheme is under finalization and upon approval and notification of 
the scheme, formal proposals would be invited and investors identified.

Winding up of NCTE  
2814. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of HU MAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government had proposed on the recommendati ons of Sudeep Banerjee 
Committee, to wind up the National Council for Teacher Education, by repealing the NCTE 
Act, 1993; and 
(b)  whether Government would re-examine its proposal to wind up the NCTE, in view of 
the impending legislation of Right to Education Bill, which calls for additional requirement 
of teachers at all levels? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) A Revie w Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Shri Sudeep Banerjee, the then Advisor Ministry of Human Resource 
Development was apponted to conduct an indepth study of the National Council for Teacher 
Education (NCTE), New Delhi and its Regional Office s. The Committee observed inter-
alia that the functioning of NCTE was not commensurate with the objective of planned and 
coordinated development of Teacher Education and recommended that the NCTE Act, 1993 
should be repealed and all regulatory functions rel ating to teacher education and teacher 
education institutions should be vested in the Univ ersity system. After inter-ministerial 
consultations the Legislative Department under the Ministry of Law & Justice has been 
requested to draft the 'Repeal Bill'.  
(b) There is no proposal to re-examine the decision to repeal the NCTE Act at present.

Reviewing the functioning of UGC and AICTE  
2827. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether the Ministry, in tune with the recommendations of the National Knowledge 
Commission has constituted a panel to review the functioning of UGC and AICTE; 
(b)  if so, what are the terms of reference of the panel  and by when it would submit its 
report; 
(c)  whether the panel would also look into the aspects of regulatory mechanism in the 
field of higher education and the contemporary changes taking place in the area of university 
education; 
(d)  if so, the details thereof; and 
(e)  if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) A Review Committee has 
been constituted by Government under the Chairmanship of Prof. Yash Pal, former Chairman, 
University Grants Commission to review the functioning of the University Grant Commission 
and the All India Council for Technical Education. The terms of reference of the Committee 
are:—  
(i) To review the functioning of the UGC/AICTE and to critically assess the role of the 
UGC/AICTE and their preparedness to provide institutional leadership to the emerging 
demands of access, equity, relevance and quality of  higher education/technical 
education and the university system.  
(ii) To review the provisions of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 and the All 
India Council for Technical Education Act, 1987 and  various suggestions for 
amendments to the said Acts by earlier Commissions such as the Prof. Amreek Singh 
Committee.  
(iii) The role of the UGC in coordinating standards  of higher education vis-a-vis the 
functional role of other statutory bodies such as A ICTE, MCI, DCI, NCI, NCTE, 
DEC, etc.  
(iv) An assessment of the requirements of autonomy of the UGC vis-a-vis the Central 
Government and that of the university system vis-a-vis the UGC.  
(v) The role of the UGC/AICTE in determining and en forcing standards of higher 
education/technical education in State Universities and the possibility of introducing 
a system of incentives and disincentives so that national standards of higher education/ 
technical education are not compromised or diluted. 
(vi) Recommendations in regard to an effective and efficient mechanism for flow of 
resources from the UGC to the universities for thei r timely utilization including a 
mechanism of feedback thereto.

(vii) The requirement of transparency and efficiency in the functioning of the UGC/AICTE.  
(viii) The role of the UGC vis-a-vis declaration of institutions to be deemed universities 
and recommendations for streamlining the process adopted by the UGC.  
(ix) Recommendations about the need to change the e ligibility criteria for becoming 
eligible to receive grants under Section 12B of the UGC Act 1956.  
(x) Any other issue arising out of or relating to t he above terms of reference and, the 
functioning of the UGC/AICTE which the Government or the Committee on its own,

The Committee is required to submit its report within a period of one year.

2828. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether there is any proposal to increase the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) for higher 
education; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof including the GER for el ementary education, high school, 
higher secondary and higher education, as on today, State-wise and category-wise; 
(c)  whether enrolment in unrecognized and non-formal institutions were also incorporated 
in the GER; 
(d)  if so, the details thereof; 
(e)  if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(f)  the steps taken thereon to achieve sustainable increase in equitable access to quality 
higher education? 
. THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RE SOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDES WARI): (a) to (f) It is proposed to increase 
the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in higher education from the present about 10% to 15% 
by the end of the Eleventh Plan. The various measur es/interventions to increase access 
equity and quality in higher education are as follo ws:  
(i) setting up of 16 Central Universities in uncove red States and 14 world class 
.universities.  
(ii) Setting up of 370 new Colleges in districts with low Gross Enrolment Ratio, including 
88 Muslim concentrated districts, in partnership with State Governments.  
(iii) Incentivising State Governments to set up/expand institutions of higher education.  
(iv) Construction of girls' hostels.  
(v) Supporting 150 uncovered State Universities and 6000 colleges.  
(vi) Reduction in regional imbalance, social gaps and promotion of inclusiveness in higher 
education.  
While computing the GER the enrolment of unrecogniz ed and non formal institutions 
was not incorporated in 2005-06 as the same is not being collected. A statement indicating 
the GER as on 30-9-2005 State-wise and category-wise is enclosed.

quality faculty from within the country and abroad to increase their faculty strength.

Suitablity of college graduates for employment  
2846. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that only 10 to 25 per cent of college graduates are suitable for 
employment and 9 per cent of graduates of the country are unfit for employment, as per 
survey conducted by the World Bank; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof; 
(c)  whether the present higher education system is merely increasing the number of degree 
holders and not professionals; 
 
(d)  if so, whether Government proposes to check out any  action plan to make higher 
education employment oriented; and 
(e)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) Government's attention 
has been drawn to a study by a non-official Consultancy Organization, which has been quoted 
by a publication of the World Bank on "Strengthening Skills and Education for Innovation". 
According to the study, only 10-25 per cent of "general college graduates in India are 
suitable for employment". The reason given by the study is that links with industry are low 
in most educational institutions, leading to curricula that allegedly do not reflect modern 
technological development or include industrial practices. However, such a conclusion cannot 
be used for generalizing preference for professional education over general higher education, 
because both general Higher Education and professional Education are significant contributors 
to the development of human resource for any society. Relevance of Higher Education is a 
continuous process. The expansion of Higher Education approved by the National 
Development Council (NDC) under the Eleventh Plan t hrough substantial increase in 
allocation and setting up of new IITs, IIMs, Central Universities and other institutions 
illustrates a balanced growth of Higher Education. The University Grants Commission (UGC) 
has redesigned its Vocational Education Programme since 2003-04 and the new Career 
Orientation Programme of the UGC, supplements relevant knowledge, skills and aptitude 
for gainful employment and self-employment to students pursuing the conventional 
undergraduate degree curriculum.

Working days of High Courts and Supreme Court  
2853. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state:  
(a)  whether the working days in High Courts and Supreme Court are less than those in the 
lower courts in the country; 
(b)  if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c)  whether Government proposes to enhance the working days of High Courts and 
Supreme Court for speedy disposal of cases; 
(d)  if so, the details thereof; and 
(e)  by when the working days are likely to be enhanced? 

78    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ ): (a) to (e) The 
working days in the Supreme Court and High Courts are regulated by the rules framed by the 
respective Courts. According to available informati on, the Supreme Court of India works 
for 222 days in a year, all High Courts in the country normally have 210 working days in a 
year and the number of working days of the District/Subordinate Courts are regulated by the 
concerned High Court.  
The Department of Justice in July, 2001 had invited the views of the High Courts regarding 
the number of working days in the High Courts and the curtailment of their vacations. Replies 
were received from 14 High Courts. The High Court o f Uttaranchal (now Uttarakhand) 
increased the number of its working days in a year from 210 to 224 and the High Court of 
Karnataka from 210 to 214. Jharkhand High Court had no objection to increasing the number 
of working days. Other High Courts had not favoured increase in the number of their working 
days.  
In the year 2002-03, this Department had examined the matter of enhancing the number 
of working days in Courts. In order to reduce the h uge pendencies prevailing in the High 
Courts, this Department addressed to all the High Courts, requesting them to fix the period 
of vacations in such a way that the number of working days of High Courts generally do not 
fall below 222 days in a year.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) The present 
system of appointment of Judges was adopted after t he Supreme Court judgment of 6th 
October, 1993 in the case of Supreme Court Advocates on Record &Ors. Vs. Union of India

India has to initiate proposal for appointment of Judges to Supreme Court and Chief Justices

was appointed on ad-hoc basis after his retirement to maintain the continuity of an important 
case which he was hearing. The cases of Himachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh High Court 
were not found in conformity with the policy. 
Reservation in judiciary  
2856. SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI:  
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that a few Members of Parliament have demanded for a quota in 
higher judicial services for candidates belonging to backward classes; 
(b)  if so, the details of action taken thereon; and 
(c)  whether it is a fact that even in lower judicial se rvices, particularly in Delhi, no 
reservation has been made for OBCs in the recruitme nt of judicial officers and if so, the 
reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to (c) Under 
article 235 of the Constitution of India, the admin istrative control over the members of 
subordinate judiciary in the States vests with the concerned High Court. Further, in exercise 
of powers conferred under proviso to article 309 re ad with article 233 and 234 of the 
Constitution, the State Government frames rules and  regulations in consultation with the 
High Court. The members of the State Judicial Servi ce are governed by these rules and 
regulations. Therefore, the service conditions, including appointment, promotion, reservations 
etc. of judicial officers of the District/Subordinate Courts are governed by the respective

State Governments. The Central Government is not concerned with any of the functions in 
this regard.  
At the High Court in Supreme Court level, the appoi ntment of the Judges of Supreme 
Court and High Courts are made under articles 124 a nd 217 of the Constitution of India 
respectively, which do not provide for reservation for any caste or class of persons. The 
Government have, however, addressed letters to the Chief Ministers of the States and the 
Chief Justices of the High Courts, from time to time, requesting them to locate persons from 
the Bar belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities 
and amongst Women who are suitable for appointment as High Court Judges.  
Increase in strength of judges  
2857. SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI:  
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government's attention has been drawn to a recent statement of Hon'ble 
Chief Justice of India to the effect that the count ry had only 12,000 Judges against the 
sanctioned strength of 14,000 and as a result there of 3.5 crores cases are pending in lower 
courts, 37 lakhs in High Courts and 46,000 in the Supreme Court; and 
(b)  if so, what action Government proposes to take to increase the strength of Judges both 
at the lower Judiciary and in the High Courts and b y when? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ ): (a) and (b) 
Government's attention to shortage of Judges and pe ndency in courts has been drawn in 
different fora. The Law Commission in its 120th Rep ort recommended that the strength of 
judges per million population may be increased from  10.5 to 50 judges. The present judge 
strength in India is 14 per million population (app rox.). Government has already increased 
the Judge strength in the High Courts by 152.  
With regard to subordinate judiciary, the Supreme Court, in its judgment of 21st March, 
2002, in All India Judges' Association & Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors., directed that an 
increase in the Judge strength from the existing 10.5 per 10 lakh people to 50 judges per 10 
lakh people should be effected and implemented with in a period of five years in a phased 
manner to be determined and directed by the Union Ministry of Law. The Central Government 
have filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court praying that the increase in judge strength in the 
Union Territories for which Central Government is administratively responsible be allowed 
based on workload and pendency of cases. The matter is sub-judice.  
All State Governments are also party to this case. Under article 235 of the Constitution of 
India, the administative control over the members o f subordinate judiciary in the States 
vests with the concerned High Court and the State G overnment. Accordingly, the Central 
Government has requested all the State Governments for taking necessary action to increase 
the judge strength as per the direction of the Supr eme Court and also to fill up the vacant 
posts of judicial officers on urgent basis.

Coal/Gas shortage in power projects 
2892. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether several power projects in the country are facing coal/gas shortages; 
(b)  whether due to coal and gas shortage, the productio n capacity of such power plants 
has come down; and 

104    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
(c) if so, the steps taken by Government to meet the shortages of gas and coal for power 
plants?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) and (b) The coal supply position to Th ermal Power Stations (TPSs) in the 
country is not comfortable. As on 14th April, 2008,  out of 77 coal based thermal power 
stations of power utilities, 24 power stations are critical having a coal stock of less than 7 days. 
The All India coal stock is also low at 10.841 Mill ion Tonne (MT) against a normative 
requirement of 22 Million Tonne.  
During 2007-08, the actual Plant Load Factor (PLF) of coal based TPSs in the country was 
78.91% against a target of 77.78%. However, according to NTPC, there was loss in PLF of 4 of 
their power stations, namely Farakka, Kahalgaon, Talcher (Kaniha) and Vindhyachal to the tune of 
4.66%, 0.65%, 0.08% and 0.33% respectively. Rigorous monitoring of supply of coal to the power 
stations is being done at all levels, for optimizing coal supply to power stations from various 
sources.  
The production and supply of gas in the country is also not keeping pace with the growing 
demand of gas in the country, including for that of power sector. The average gas supply during 
2007-08 (April-February 2008) has been 37.06 MMSCMD, against the requirement of 65.67 
MMSCMD to operate the stations at 90% PLF.  
(c) Following steps have been taken/are being taken  by the Government to meet the 
shortages of gas and coal for power stations:  
(i) Rigorous monitoring of supply of coal to thermal power stations for optimizing coal 
supply to the power stations from various sources.  
(ii) Ministry of Coal is being insisted upon to enhance the production of coal in the 
country.  
(iii) Import of coal to meet the shortfall in domestic availability of coal.  
(iv) Arranging spot Regasified Liquified Natural Gas (RLNG).  
(v) New coal blocks are being  located by the Ministry of Coal to power producers/ utilities 
for captive mining to meet requirement of their power plants.  
Bringing the Power Sector to International level  
†2893.   DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:  
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that the present shortage of power in the country can be solved by 
bringing the present power distribution and transmission losses and the quantum of power 
generation (Plant Load Factor) of power generating projects at international level; 
(b)  if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(c)  the quantum of availability of additional power to be achieved in the country as a result 
of bringing the level of both the above power sectors at international level? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  

Written Answers to  [21 APRIL 2008]  Unstarred Questions    105  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) to (c) The present (April 2007 to March 2008) shortage of power in the country 
in terms of energy and peak is 72,392 million units (9.8%) and 18,073 MW (16.6%) respectively. 
The transmission and distribution (T&D) losses in the country during the year 2006-07 were 
28.65% (provisional). The T&D losses in developed countries is in the range of 6 to 11%. It has 
not been possible to segregate technical and commercial losses in the absence of complete 
energy audit, consumer indexing, availability of IT facilities etc., in most States. As such, the 
additional energy which can become available as a result of reduction of technical losses in the 
transmission and distribution system, cannot be estimated at present. Efforts are afoot to put an 
energy audit system in place in the distribution segment through the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP).

Joint venture of NTPC and BHEL  
2896. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether the Central Government proposes to create a separate company, namely, NTPC-
BHEL Power Project Private Limited; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof; and 
(c)  the reasons for starting such a company in view of the fact that BHEL already exists? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): 
(a) Yes, Sir. NTPC Ltd. is in the process of formation of a Joint Venture Company (JVC) with BHEL. 
Memorandum of Understanding, Joint Venture Agreement and a Supplementary Agreement has 
been signed and Registrar of Companies is being approached for allotting the name of the JV 
Company.  
(b)  The JVC would carry out Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contracts for 
Power Plants and other Infrastructure Projects as well as manufacture and supply equipments for 
power plants and other infrastructure projects in India and abroad including plant engineering, project 
management, quality insurance, quality control, procurement, logistics, site management, erection 
and commissioning services. The JVC shall have an initial authorized and paid up capital of Rs. 5 
crore equally subscribed by the initial promoters  viz.  BHEL and NTPC Ltd. 
(c)  Considering the large capacity addition plan in the country during the 11th and 12th Five Year 
Plans, there is a need to expand the domestic power equipment manufacturing capability as well as to 
strengthen the related manufacturing activities including Balance of Plant (BOP) etc. EPC for power 
plant and other infrastructure projects is another area which needs further expanion. NTPC Ltd. and 
BHEL intend to leverage their respective strengths and synergies to set up manufacturing facilities of 
energy related equipments for generation of power and also for taking up EPC of power plants and 
other infratructure project. Accordingly, NTPC Ltd. and BHEL intend to work jointly to complement 
their respective strengths through formation of a JVC.

2901. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:

getting nearly half the quantity of gas from Panna- Mukta-Tapti fields for producing more

(c)  what are the barriers in accepting the Ministry's legitimate demand?

plants, Ministry of Power has requested Ministry of  Petroleum and Natural Gas to advise

2902. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that domestic industrial produ ction would be hampered by upto 
thirty five per cent in the coming months due to po wer shortage; 
(b)  if so, Government's response thereto; and 
(c)  the details of steps taken or proposed to be taken by Government for generation of 
more power in the country, to fulfil the industry's demand? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) to (c) There is a continuing shortage of power in the country. The quantum 
of shortage varies from State to State, on day to day and hour to hour depending on demand 
and supply of power. The energy and peak shortage in the country during the year 2007-08 
was 9.8% and 16.6% respectively.  
There is no representation from the domestic industries about the impact of power shortage 
or its impact degree in terms on the domestic production in the coming months. Electricity 
being a concurrent subject under the Constitution, the supply and distribution of electricity

2903. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that the special duty allowance and benefit to officers in National 
Hydro Power Corporation (NHPC) was given from 1st August, 1997 whereas the Teesta Hydro 
Electric Project, Ranjit Power Station and other North Eastern Projects workers have been given

Electrification of villages  
2905. SHRIMATI BR1NDA KARAT: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government has fixed the target of electrify 1.25 lakh villages and 2.3 crore 
Below Poverty Line (BPL) households by the terminal year 2008-09 and whether an official 
assessment revealed that only 38,525 villages and 6 .73 lakhs BPL households could be 
covered by the end of March, 2007; 
(b)  what have been the major reasons for such huge gaps in targets and achievements in 
this regard; and 
(c)  what steps Government is taking to speed up the process of implementation so that the 
targets can be achieved within the stipulated time-frame? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government under its ambitious programme of Rajiv Gandhi 
Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) as part of Bhar at Nirman has envisaged 
electrification of about 1.25 lakh villages as well as providing electricity connection to 2.3 
crore Below Poverty Line (BPL) households in the country by 2009. By the end of March, 
2007, electrification of 38,525 unelectrified villages and intensive electrification of 11,877 
already electrified villages have been completed. 7 ,31,527 rural households including 
6,72,588 BPL households were provided electricity connections by March, 2007.  
(b) The following issues have affected smooth implementation of the programme:  
(i) Delay in receipt of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs).  
(ii) Delay in forest clearance.  

Written Answers to  [21 APRIL 2008]  Unstarred Questions    123  
(iii) Delays in land acquisition for 33/11 KV sub-stations.  
(iv) Limited number of good agencies able to execute turnkey jobs.  
(v)  Very high rates quoted by contracting agencies.  
(vi) Shortage of material and increased prices.  
(vii)  Delays in the issue of road permit and way bills.  
(viii) Delays in taking over of physical assets cre ated by Central Public Sector 
Undertakings (CPSUs) under RGGVY by State utilities .  
(ix)Delays in Panchayat certificates for vilage electrification as per revised definition.  
(x) Lack of awareness among villagers for taking new connections.  
(xi) Very poor upstream rural electricity infrastructure in some States.  
(xii)  Delay in finalisation of BPL lists by some States.  
(xiii)  Refusal to waive State and local taxes on materials by some States.  
(xiv)  Difficult terrain in some cases.  
(c) To achieve the targets within the stipulated time-frame, the following steps have been taken:  
(i) Government of India has set up an inter-Ministerial Monitoring Committee which periodically 
meets to sanction projects and review progress of implementation.  
(ii) States have been advised to set up district Co mmittees to monitor the progress of rural 
electrification works. All the States have notified formation of district Committees.  
(iii) The Government of India as also Rural Electrification Corporation (REC), the nodal agency 
for RGGVY, conduct frequent review meetings with al l the stakeholders; the concerned 
State Governments, State power utilities and implem enting agencies for expeditious 
implementation of the scheme on the agreed schedules.  
(iv) For speedier and effective implementation of projects, their execution has been taken up on 
turnkey basis.  
(v) Decentralized Distributed Generation (DDG) and Supply has been brought under the ambit of 
RGGVY  
(vi) To ensure qualitative execution of rural electrification works, a three tier quality control 
mechanism has been enforced under RGGVY.  
(vii) Grant amount of BPL connection has been enhanced to Rs. 2200/- from Rs. 1500/-. 
(viii) To take car of the cost escalation, cost norms for village electrification has been revised 
upward as given below:—

†2911. SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that compensation and employment to the families whose land has

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHR I JAIRAM 
RAMESH): (a) and (b) No, Sir. Land for Sipat Thermal Power Project was acquired by the 
State Government of the undivided Madhya Pradesh for NTPC according to the provisions 
of Land Acquisition Act. The first notification under Section 4 of the Act for the priority area 
was notified on 06.11.1998. Subsequent notifications for other areas followed. The Entire 
compensation for the acquired assets, as decided by the State Government, has been deposited 
with the State Government for further distribution of the same.  
In addition to the entitled compensation, NTPC initiated activities for the Resettlement 
and Rehabilitation (R & R) of the Project Affected Persons (PAPs) in accordance with its 
company policy right since inception. A Socio Economic Survey (SES) was conducted by 
IIT Kanpur in 1998 for all the affected villages. S ubsequent to the completion of SES, 
formulation of a comprehensive Rehabilitation Action Plan (RAP) was initiated in consultation 
with the State Government and the PAPs.

A comprehensive RAP was formulated for Sipat projec t through a participative and 
consultative process incorporating suggestions made  by PAPs their representatives, local 
representative and officials from the state government in various consultation meetings. The 
RAP so formulated was finally approved by the District Collector Bilaspur on 9.8.2000 for 
implementation. Having gone through the entire process and the Government of Chhattisgarh 
having approved it. NTPC is committed to the agreed  RAP in its entirety as approved by 
Government of Chhattisgarh. The salient RAP provisions are as follows:- Individual R&R 
benefits in the form of grants to land owner PAP to  facilitate purchase of land for land 
considered as a prime rehabilitation measure.  
—  Grants to other categoreis of PAPs namely those tilling government land, allottees 
of lndira AvasYojana etc.  , 
—  40% shop allotment to PAPs in the township 
—  Community development activities including infrastracture upgradation in the 
project affected villages. 
—  Grants to Village Panchayats for a definite period. 
—  Other facilities like capacity building, employment opportunities and welfare 
related activities. 
NTPC has reported that all the activities to be executed by NTPC, as envisaged in RAP, 
have been completed.  
As regards employment opportunities, there was no s uch agreement of providing direct 
employment to PAPs in NTPC. As the Sipat Thermal Power Project is being installed largely 
with environment friendly super critical technology .it was categorically mentioned in the 
RAP that employment opportunities shall be comparat ively less. However, for direct 
employment in NTPC in the unskilled category, only PAPs would be considered and in the 
skilled category preference would be given to them subject to availability of vacancies. Till 
now, 43 PAPs have been recruited in skilled category and recruitment of 100 PAPs in unskilled 
category is under process. Further 2042 PAPs/Local persons have been deployed under 
contracting agencies engaged for construction activities in the project.  
As and when further vacancies are notified. PAPs would be considered for employment 
in accordance with the provisions of the comprehensive and agreed RAP.

kept at the disposal of the Central Government, is reviewed and revised from time to time

get allocation from the Central Generating Stations programmed to be commissioned during 
the Eleventh Plan period in accordance with the existing guidelines.

Reservation for Scheduled Castes  
†2919. SHRI KRISHAN LAL BALMIKI: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that a commission has been constituted by the Central Government 
on the subject of reservation for Scheduled Castes; 
(b)  whether there is a provision to provide special opportunity by fixing a separate quota 
for the communities among the Scheduled Castes who have not been able to take benefit of 
reservation, after the constitution of this commission; 
(c)  whether all castes could not get the benefit of the  reservation system for Scheduled

EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): (a) The Government 
of India has set up a National Commission to examin e the issue of Sub-Categorisation of

(i) To examine the various facts of the demand for sub-categorization of Scheduled 
Castes in Andhra Pradesh subsequent to the judgement of the Supreme Court of 
India in the case of E.V. Chinnaiah Vs State of Andhra Pradesh & others [2004(9)

for sub-categorisation of Scheduled Castes.

grounds and the criteria on which these recommendations are based.  
(c) & (d) The endeavour is to bring about over all development of Scheduled Castes 
listed in the Presidential Orders made under Article 341(1) of the Constitution of India and 
amended from time to time by Acts of Parliament under Article 341(2) of the Constitution.

Poverty among tribals  
2928. SHRI PENUMALLI MADHU: Will the Minister of TRIBALAFFAIRS be pleased 
to state:  
(a)  the present criteria adopted by Government to identify poverty among tribals; and 
(b)  what are the steps to help the tribals having marginal land holdings who are deprived 
of the BPL benefits because of the present criteria being dubious? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TRIBAL AFF AIRS (DR. 
RAMESHWAR ORAON): (a) The Planning Commission estimates the incidence of poverty 
at national level and State level from the large sa mple surveys on Household Consumer 
expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) after an interval 
of approximately five years according to the method ology contained in the Report of the 
Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor. The percentage of people 
living below the poverty line among the Scheduled Tribe population are estimated from the 
percentage distribution of Scheduled Tribe persons as obtained from the above Survey of 
Consumer Expenditure and poverty line of all population. While the estimation of incidence 
of poverty is done by Planning Commission and ident ification of the poor is done by the 
State Governments in association with the Ministry of Rural Development, identification of 
the poor is done by the State Governments in associ ation with the Ministry of Rural 
Development. Further, the Ministry of Rural Development conducts the Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) Census in rural areas to identify the BPL households who could be targeted under its 
various programmes. The last BPL Census conducted i n 2002 was based on score based 
ranking of rural household and had 13 socio-economi c parameters including various sizes 
of land holdings.

Malnutrition and related problems  
2932. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA:  
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government's attention has been drawn towards recently published UNICEF 
report "the State of the World's Children" in which it has been stated that daily 5,700 children 
die due to malnutrition and related problem; 
(b)  whether Government are also aware that 46 per cent of Indian children are victims of 
malnutrition; 
(c)  if so, whether Government has evaluated existing schemes related to children and has 
done any social audit; and 
(d)  if so, the results thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHR1MATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) As per UNICEF's Report 
"the State of the World's Children - 2008", every day on average more than 26,000 children 
under the age of five die around the world, mostly from preventable causes.  
(b)  42.5% children under five in the country are underweight as reported under National 
Family Health Survey - III (2005-2006) conducted by  Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare. 
(c)  and (d) An Appraisal of three decades of ICDS was conducted by National Institute of 
Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD) i n 2006. The study covered 150 
ICDS Projects from 35 States/UTs covering rural, urban and tribal projects. 

Written Answers to  [21 APRIL 2008]  Unstarred Questions    153  
The main findings of the appraisal are as under:  
* Around 59 per cent AWCs studied have no toilet faci lity and in 17 AWCs this 
facility was found to be unsatisfactory; 
* Around 75% of AWCs have pucca buildings; 
* 44 per cent AWCs covered under the study were found to be lacking PSE kits: 
* Disruption of supplementary nutrition was noticed on an average of 46.31 days at 
Anganwadi level. Major reasons causing disruption was reported as delay in supply 
of items of supplementary nutrition; 
* 36.5 per cent mothers did not report weighing of new born children; 
* 29 per cent children were born with a low weight which was below normal (less 
than 2500 gm); 
* 37 per cent AWWs reported non-availability of materials/aids for Nutrition and 
Health Education (NHED). 
Stiffer Anti-dowry Laws  
2933. SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR:  
SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN:  
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government intends to make anti-dowry laws stiffer; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof and the recommendations of the National Commission for 
Women in this regard; 
(c)  whether it is a fact that courts have gone on recor d stating that the dowry laws are 
absued to a large extent; and 
(d)  if so, the safeguards being considered to prevent the above of dowry laws? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b ) National 
Commission for Women has made some recommendations for the amendment of the Dowry 
Prohibition Act, 1961 and Section 304B IPC (dowry d eath). The main points of the 
recommendations are given in the enclosed statement (See below).  
(c) and (d) The Ministry does not have any informat ion on misuse of dowry laws to a 
large extent.  
Statement  
Main Points of Recommendations of National Commission for Women.  
The National Commission for women has made the following main recommendations:—  
(i) The words 'in connection with the marriage of said parties' occurring in section 2 of the 
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 relating to the definition of dowry, may be deleted.  

154    Written Answers to  [RAJYASABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
(ii) The penalty laid down in the said Act for givi ng dowry may be reduced to 
imprisonment of not less than one year and fine of not less than Rs. 15,000/-
unless the person can prove that he was compelled to give dowry;  
(iii) Amend section 6 of the said Act (dowry to be for the benefit of the wife or her 
heirs) in order to provide that in the event of the death of any  woman, whether due 
to natural causes or otherwise, whether within 7 ye ars or after 7 years of her 
marriage, any property to which she is entitled under the section will be transferred 
to her children or to her parents if she has no children.  
(iv) Amend section 4 (1) (a) to provide for jurisdiction of courts.  
(v) Empower the Service Provider or the Protection Officer functioning under the 
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 200 5, under section 7 of 
the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, to lodge a complai nt of commission of an 
offence.  
(vi) The words 'soon before her death' occurring in  sub-section (1) of section 304B 
IPC (dowry death) may be replaced by the words 'anytime before her death' and 
any death occurring in the circumstances mentioned in the sub-section even after 
7 years of marriage should be considered as dowry d eath. The minimum 
punishment laid down in the sub-section (2) of section 304B IPC should be raised 
from 7 years to 10 years and death may be prescribe d as the maximum penalty 
alternate to the existing penalty of imprisonment for life.

MATTERS RAISED WITH PERMISSION  
Loss to standing crops due to untimely heavy rains particularly in Maharashtra  
SHRI SANJAY RAUT (Maharashtra): Sir, I rise to draw  the attention of this august 
House towards the pathetic condition of farmers of the country, especially of Maharashtra 
State due to untimely heavy rains during the last month.   - 
Two districts, namely, Sindhudurg and Ratnagiri in Konkan region and four districts of 
Marathwada region, namely Aurangabad, Jalna, Latur and Usmanabadh, were lashed away 
by these untimely heavy rains last month. Sir, mango and cashew crops, which were almost 
ripened and ready to be taken to market were destroyed by these heavy rains. A pest called 
Anthracnose, which spoiled the mango crop with blan d stains on them, has badly affected 
the mango crop this time. Sir, what to talk about the export houses, even the small traders are 
not wiling to purchase these black stained mangoes.  The total loss to mango growers is 
estimated in crores. Also, the heavy untimely rains  in Marathwada region have damaged 
standing crops of wheat, jawar and sugarcane. The crop of orange, which is main fruit grown 
by horticulturists of Marathwada region, has also been damaged heavily.  
Sir, I, therefore, request the hon. Agriculture Min ister, who himself is a farmer and an 
expert on the subject, to announce immediate adequate financial relief to the farmers of Konkan 
and Marathwada regions who have lost their crops due to this natural calamity. Thank you.

Damage caused to the Indian traders in UAE due to fire at RN Market, Dubai and  need to 
extend help to them  
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would like to request the 
Government, through you, to take some steps in order to help the poor victims of fire that broke out in 
Dubai. On 2nd April, one of the oldest traditional souk of Dubai, the Old Naif Souk, was destroyed 
by the inferno. Out of 330 shops in that particular market, 250 are owned by the non-resident Indians. 
Majority of them are from Kerala. Nearly eight hundred -workers from Kerala also lost their livelihood. 
The UAE authorities have already announced temporary resettlement programmes, which will take 
some months in implementation. The workers, who are nearly eight hundred in number, are living in a 
very pathetic condition. They are somehow living only because of the help extended by some social 
organisations. Nearly 100 workers also lost their passports in the fire accident. In such a situation, 
our embassy in the UAE has to take some initiatives to provide assistance to the workers. The 
embassy has to coordinate a relief programme for all the 800 workers till the rehabilitation process is 
over. Also, the Indian authorities are asking for a regular fee for new passports, which is nearly Rs. 
7,000—Rs. 5,000 for application and Rs. 2,000 as processing fee—from the workers who have lost 
their passports in the fire accident. Considering the pathetic condition of the workers the Government 
of India has to direct our embassy in the UAE to waive the charges for the new passports. Passports, 
without any fee, should be issued to the poor workers only then they would be able to try for some other 
employment and come back to India. So, in such a situation, all these steps should be taken by the 
Government of India. Necessary instructions from the Ministry should be issued to our Ambassador 
in the UAE and to our Counsellor General in Dubai to take all the necessary steps to extend assistances 
to the poor Indian traders and workers who have been affected by the fire.

DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Sir, according to the NCRB, on as average,

ticks by in India, inflicts more brutality on women, with two rapes, two kidnappings, four molestations 
and seven incidents of cruelty by husbands and relatives.

for 13 per cent of total incidents in 2006, Uttar Pradesh was a close second with

Need to install a statue of Lukhy Shah Vanjara  
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (Haryana): Sir, my special Mention is regarding having a 
statue of Shri Lukhy Shah Vanjara.  
It is recorded in the history that the entire land on which the present Parliament Complex, 
Secretariat and Rashtrapati Bhawan are situated belonged to Shri Lukhy Shah Vanjara who 
was responsible for organising the cremation of the body of Guru Tegh Bahadur in November, 
1675. Everyone is aware that for the sake of freedo m of worship to everyone, Guru Tegh 
Bahadurji, the Ninth Guru of the Sikhs, sacrificed his life and was beheaded in Chandni 
Chowk during the time of Emperor Aurangzeb. Lukhy Shah took the courage of lifting the 
body and bringing to his village and burnt his house to cremate the body. Gurdwara Rakab 
Ganj was built on that place. The whole of the village land was donated for the Gurdwara, 
and, in 1915, the British Government took the land for buil ding the above-mentioned 
complexes. I request that a statue of Lukhy Shah Vanjara should be installed at a suitable  

172 Special  [RAJYA SABHA]  Mentions  
place to honour the sacrifice made by him. It is unfortunate that we have a road in the name 
of Aurangzeb, but nothing in the name of Guru Tegh Bahadur and his disciple Lukhy Shah 
Vanjara.

DR. E.M. SUDARSANANATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank 
you for giving me this opportunity to speak. Sir, really, I am proud of having participated in 
this debate. For the first time the fund from the Government of India for the Rural Development 
Ministry has come nearer to the top second, next to  the Defence Ministry. No doubut, one 
day it may also overtake the first one and will be having first rank so that the entire India can 
develop on a fast track. When the NDA Government wa s ruling, they were allotting very 
meagre amount for the rural development. Take for e xample, for 2001-02, they allotted 
about Rs. 11,000 crores, for 2002-03, they allotted Rs. 18,203 crores, and for 2003-04, they 
allotted Rs. 19,228 crores. Immediately after assuming power, the UPA Government under 
the guidance of Madam Sonia Gandhi and great leadership of Dr. Manmohan Singh, it could 
raise the allotment for rural development to Rs. 18,167 crores (?) and immediately next year 
Rs. 27,489 crores were allotted. For 2006-07, Rs. 39982 crores were allotted. Sir, in 2007-
08, Rs. 36,560 crores were allotted. Now it has gal loped to Rs. 49,450 crores. So much of 
money is now pumped towards development. Sir, right  from the days of Independence, 
Mahatma Gandhi was telling that you have to remember the Gram Rajya, that is, Ram Rajya. 
If you develop villages and the poor man who is living in the countryside, that development 
of India will be the real one and that will be Suswraj. It has been the approach of our Five 
year Plans. Even after developing irrigation and new methods of agriculture, the poverty in 
the rural areas could not be attacked. But Indira G andhi brought the 20-Point Programme 
and she made the poor as the target group so that they could cross the poverty line. Therefore, 
she brought a great programme, the national Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. Through 
that programme, every person can get employment and  community assets can be created 
through that fund. Subsequently, it was developed into Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme 
Programme (REGP), where an assurance was given for hundred days to an individual who is 
ready to work, who is ready to use his physical energy for creation of assets, was implemented. 
But Sir, even though the Government of India at the  National level allocated some money 
and programmes, it has to go through the system which we have created in the Constitution, 
i.e. the State Governments. When it goes to the State Go vernments, it has to percolate into 
the villages and into the hands of the poor people. We could not succeed there. Just like an 
overhead tank, which is filled up with water has to go down to the pipeline; somebody has to 
open the pipe. Then, that pipe has to bring water to the roads and also to the roadside and to 
the houses. Then, only the water, which is filled u p in the overhead tanks, can be useful, 
Similarly, the Central Government has allotted money but nobody is there to open the tap so

that water can go down to the streets and also to t he houses. Then, it happened. Then State 
Governments have to have the onerous duty of bringing money to the ordinary person. Then, 
only Madam, Indira Gandhi brought this system of ha ving Rural Employment Guarantee 
Scheme Programme at that time. Subsequently, when Rajiv Gandhi became the Prime Minister, 
he went to the villages and found first hand inform ation, of how one rupee, which is sent 
from the Central Government, reaches as 15 paise to the villages. Now, in Orissa, even now, 
only 10 paise is going. How that money goes, where it goes, where that 90 paise has gone 
was a question raised by Rajiv Gandhiji. Then, only he found that Panchayati Raj system has 
to be started and the people who are living in poverty, who are living in the villages have to 
be empowered by giving power to them. He has done it. I was at that time a Mandal Chairman, 
i.e. Panchayati Chairman at that time. I could see how t he Panchayat Presidents were very 
happy to receive a draft in their name from Central Government by the name of Rajiv Gandhi. 
That Rs. 2 lakh is sent according to the population , Rs. 15 lakh is sent according to the 
population and the villages can sit and decide for which purpose this money can be utilised. 
That was the empowerment given by Shri Rajiv Gandhi and he wanted to make it as part of 
the Constitution itself, he made an effort to amend  the Constitution so that the three-tier 
system should be in existence. But, that was not accepted by certain States and also certain 
parties. Therefore, he met with a failure but the subsequent Governments — even though it 
was not fully as efficient as Rajiv Gandhi — did no t enact it but it was enacted in some way 
by creating a four tier system, i.e. the village level Panchayat i.e. the Zilla Panchayat, and 
intermediate level and the Panchayat level. But, no w this three-tier system is in existence. 
Now, the system is, Sir, how much money the State G overnments are allotting for rural 
development? They are fully depending upon the Cent ral Government aids. They want to 
see that the money has to come from overhead tanks.  They need not dig their own pipes 
there itself. They need not have their bore wells t here itself. They don't want to have their 
own well there itself. They want to get the money from the overhead tanks. Somebody has to 
pump the money and the, they can spend from that. S ir, that is the situation now. Now, we 
have implemented lot of schemes in the rural areas, they are massive agricultural programmes. 
Such are the programmes. That was a very important programme on which the ordinary 
agriculturist can cultivate his own land and the money ...(Interruptioons)... utilised from the 
Central Government fund... (Interruptions)... and the money can be utilised from the Central 
Government for ordinary peasants in remote villages . He could enjoy that money. That 
exchequers' expenditure can be utilised for cultivating his own land, for reclaiming his own 
land. He can get very good irrigation facilities through that method. He can dig it in his own 
land. This is all was done during Shri Rajiv Gandhi 's period. Sir, during that period, Rs. 1 
lakh was given to people belonging to Dalit communi ties for getting a motor pump set so 
that they can pump water and irrigate their own lan d. If, in a community, ten people are 
united together, they can also avail of this facility. That was the vision of Shri Rajiv Gandhiji. 
Of course, everything was done through the Governme nt orders. When the Government 
changed and a new Government took over the office, it ignored rural development. They 
never cared about the rural people. They never cared about development. They never cared 
about the poverty alleviation programmes. They were worried only to construct a 'big road' 
and sell it to contractors. Take for example, they enacted the Road Cess Act, 2000, and, 
through this legislation, they collected money from everybody and spent a certain percentage 
of money for the development of roads only in urban areas. They never thought that the Act 
should have a provision for rural areas and certain amount of money should be given for the 
development of villages. They never thought about it. They never allocated money for rural 
development. Finally, there was one programme. I do n't want to hide that. There was a
